# PitCrew how-to guides

Task guides for PitCrew. Each guide says when you need it, the steps, and how to tell it worked. For
every command, setting and file, see the [reference](reference.md).

## Hold the cache while away

**When you need it:** you step away from a session with a long context and want to come back to a
warm cache. When a session sits idle for an hour, its one-hour prompt cache expires, and the next
turn writes the whole context to the cache again.

1. In that session, run:

   ```
   /pitcrew:cache-watch on
   ```

   It starts only when the session's main thread writes one-hour cache entries. It refuses a session
   with five-minute entries, or with no cache entry yet, and says why. cache-watch keeps only the
   main thread's cache: a session whose main thread writes five-minute entries is refused even when
   its subagents write one-hour entries. The main thread's TTL is Claude Code's setting for the
   session; subagent TTL settings do not change the decision.
2. Leave the session idle. After every turn, a `Stop` hook waits in the background and wakes the
   session `lead` minutes (5 by default) before the cache would expire, and no later than 52.5
   minutes after the last request. The woken turn keeps the cache for another hour.

   The agent sends one line, such as `Cache kept until 15:30 · wake 1 of 5 · reply stop to stop
   keeping it`, as a push notification and ends the turn without a reply, so the line shows once.
   The push reaches your phone when the session has Remote Control on and "Push when Claude decides"
   enabled in `/config`. Only a session without the push tool gets the line as a reply instead. With
   a `lead` up to 7, wakes come every 52.5 minutes; with a larger `lead`, every `60 - lead` minutes.
3. Any message you send in the session resets the count. After `max` wakes (5 by default) in a row
   without a message from you, watching stops. To stop earlier, reply `stop` or run
   `/pitcrew:cache-watch off`. Ending the session also stops it, and so does a compaction, manual or
   automatic: the compacted context starts a new cache, so a wake would keep nothing. `status` then
   shows `off (compacted)`; run `on` again to watch the compacted session.

What it cannot do:

- It keeps only one-hour cache entries. When the main thread switches to five-minute entries,
  watching stops, one wake tells you so, and `status` shows `off (five-minute cache)`. See [one-hour
  entries only](limitations.md#cache-watch-keeps-only-one-hour-cache-entries) and [the
  self-stop](limitations.md#cache-watch-stops-itself-when-the-main-thread-switches-to-five-minute-entries).
- It keeps only the main thread's cache. A finished subagent that you resume after its cache expired
  starts cold. See [main thread only](limitations.md#cache-watch-keeps-only-the-main-threads-cache).
- It refuses a session with no cache entry yet. See [a cache entry
  first](limitations.md#cache-watch-needs-a-cache-entry-first).
- A computer that sleeps past the cache's expiry misses the wake and loses the cache. cache-watch
  then turns off, `status` shows `off (cache expired before the wake)`, and your next message brings
  a one-line notice. See
  [sleep](limitations.md#a-computer-that-sleeps-past-the-caches-expiry-loses-the-cache).
- It keeps no cache in `claude -p` runs. See [non-interactive
  runs](limitations.md#cache-watch-does-nothing-in-non-interactive-runs).
- Without Remote Control and "Push when Claude decides", no push reaches your phone. See [the
  push](limitations.md#the-push-reaches-a-phone-only-with-remote-control).
- In a terminal session whose context is at or above the idle compaction threshold, Claude Code is
  expected to compact the conversation about 54 minutes after the last request. When the wakes run
  out, Claude Code can compact the session about 54 minutes after the last wake. See [idle
  compaction after the last
  wake](limitations.md#idle-compaction-can-run-after-cache-watchs-last-wake) and [Choose between
  cache-watch and idle compaction](#choose-between-cache-watch-and-idle-compaction).

A wake keeps the cache for far less than losing it costs. The woken turn reads the context from the
cache; the first turn after the cache's expiry writes the whole context to the cache again, which by
[Anthropic's API prices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#prompt-caching)
costs at least 20 times the read (a one-hour cache write is 2 times the input price, a cache read
0.1 times or less). Each wake still counts against the five-hour limit; how much a cache read weighs
in subscription limits is not published. With the defaults, that is at most five wakes per absence;
see [each wake counts against the five-hour
limit](limitations.md#each-wake-counts-against-the-five-hour-limit).

The defaults live in `<state>/cache-watch.json` and are the same in every session on this machine.
To change them, run `/pitcrew:cache-watch config --lead 10 --max 3`; to change them for one session,
pass the same options to `on`.

**How to tell it worked:** `/pitcrew:cache-watch status` shows the session as `on`, with the cache
expiry and the next wake, for example `<session id> · on · lead 5 min · wakes 0/5 · cache 1h ·
expires 15:30 · next wake 15:22`.

## Recover after a compaction

**When you need it:** a session was compacted, and you or the agent need what the summary dropped.
context-watch is on from install, so this works without setup.

1. Before the compaction, context-watch watches the context. When the context first passes 85% and
   then 95% of the auto-compaction point, the agent is told once per level to write its recovery
   point to the task's status file. The levels reset after each compaction. With `--line on`,
   context-watch also puts a line such as `context: 612k / 967k auto-compact point (63%)` on every
   prompt; the line is off by default.
2. At each compaction of the main conversation, automatic or `/compact`, PitCrew writes
   `.claude/pitcrew/<session id>.md` in the project. It holds your last 3 prompts, the agent's last
   2 replies, the last 5 tool calls with their inputs cut to 200 characters (without results), and
   every file the agent wrote or edited in the session.
3. The summary is told to keep the snapshot path. Right after the compaction, the agent is told to
   read the snapshot and the task's status files before its next step.
4. To read a snapshot yourself, open the file. `/pitcrew:context-watch status` prints the project's
   snapshot folder.

context-watch never vetoes, delays, or starts a compaction, and leaves subagent compactions alone.
An error in context-watch leaves the turn as it was. With auto-compaction off, the line measures
against the context window, and no warnings come. Snapshots older than 14 days are removed when a
session starts in the project; the same goes for `*.md` files older than that in
`.claude/paceline/`, where PaceLine kept its snapshots. Nothing else in either folder is touched.

**How to tell it worked:** after a compaction, `/pitcrew:context-watch status` counts the snapshot,
for example `snapshots: /home/me/project/.claude/pitcrew (1 file)`, and the agent's next step starts
by reading it.

## Change context-watch's levels, line and snapshot days

**When you need it:** the warnings come too early or too late for how you work, you want the context
figure on every prompt, or snapshots should stay for a shorter or longer time.

1. See what is set now:

   ```
   /pitcrew:context-watch status
   ```

   The first line shows the switch, the line, the warning levels and the snapshot days. `settings:`
   names the file the settings are written to. When the settings are still read from PaceLine's
   file, the last line says `(from PaceLine)`.
2. Change what you need. Each option applies alone:

   ```
   /pitcrew:context-watch config --levels 80,90
   /pitcrew:context-watch config --line on
   /pitcrew:context-watch config --days 30
   /pitcrew:context-watch config --off
   ```

   Levels are ascending whole percents from 50 to 99, and snapshots are kept 1 to 90 days. `--off`
   turns off the warnings, the line and the snapshots; `--on` turns them on again.
3. Send your next prompt. A change applies from the next prompt.

A change writes the whole settings object to PitCrew's own file, `<state>/context-watch.json`, with
the values you did not change taken from what was read, including PaceLine's. PaceLine's files are
never written, moved or deleted.

**How to tell it worked:** `config` prints one line with the new values, for example `context-watch
on · line off · warn at 80%, 90% of the auto-compact point · snapshots kept 14 days`, and `status`
shows `settings:` with PitCrew's file and no `(from PaceLine)` line.

## Choose between cache-watch and idle compaction

**When you need it:** you are leaving a session with a long context and wonder whether to hold its
cache with cache-watch, to let Claude Code compact it while it is idle, or to do neither.

The two work differently. cache-watch wakes the session before its one-hour cache expires, so the
whole history stays warm and nothing is summarized. Idle compaction is Claude Code's own behaviour:
in a terminal session whose context is at or above a token threshold, Claude Code is expected to
compact the conversation about 54 minutes after the last request ([Claude Code, settings
reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#idlecompaction), read 2026-10-15). The
threshold is 200,000 tokens unless `CLAUDE_CODE_IDLE_COMPACT_MIN_TOKENS` sets it, and idle
compaction also needs Claude Code to fetch feature flags from Anthropic, so a given session may
differ.

They meet at the end of the wakes. cache-watch wakes the session no later than 52.5 minutes after
the last request, which is before idle compaction, and each wake, as a new request, restarts Claude
Code's idle count. When the wakes run out and nobody replies, cache-watch turns itself off, and
Claude Code can compact the session about 54 minutes after the last wake.

| Your absence | Better choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| You are back within the wakes and need the whole history, not a summary. | cache-watch | The history stays in a warm cache. With the defaults, 5 wakes about 52.5 minutes apart cover about 4.4 hours. |
| You are away longer than the wakes cover. | Idle compaction, or neither | When the wakes run out, cache-watch turns off and the cache expires. Idle compaction, where it applies, then replaces the history with a summary; without it, the next turn writes the whole context to the cache again. |
| A summary of the history is enough for the work you resume. | Idle compaction, or neither | A compaction costs one summary instead of five wakes, and a wake counts against the five-hour limit. |
| The five-hour limit is tight. | Neither, or fewer wakes | Each wake is a turn. Lower `--max`, or leave cache-watch off. |

1. To hold the cache, run `/pitcrew:cache-watch on` in the session. To cover a longer absence, raise
   the number of wakes, for example:

   ```
   /pitcrew:cache-watch on --max 8
   ```

   Each wake counts against the five-hour limit.
2. To leave the session to idle compaction, do not turn cache-watch on. Where idle compaction
   applies, it needs no setting.
3. To let nothing compact the session while it is idle, do not turn cache-watch on, and set
   `idleCompaction` to `false` in Claude Code's settings (Claude Code v2.1.290 or later); on an
   earlier version, set `autoCompactEnabled` to `false`. The same source describes both settings,
   read 2026-10-15. Auto-compaction off also stops context-watch's warnings.

**How to tell it worked:** with cache-watch on, `/pitcrew:cache-watch status` shows the next wake.
When the wakes ran out, it shows `off (no reply after 5 wakes)`, and Claude Code can then compact
the session about 54 minutes later. See [idle compaction after the last
wake](limitations.md#idle-compaction-can-run-after-cache-watchs-last-wake).

## Run only one copy of the watchers while PaceLine has its own

**When you need it:** PaceLine 0.6.0 or an earlier version is installed beside PitCrew. Both carry
context-watch, so each prompt past a warning level gets two warnings and each compaction writes two
snapshots.

PitCrew reads PaceLine's `context-watch.json` and `cache-watch.json` only while it has no file of
its own with that name. Turning PaceLine's copy off first would therefore turn PitCrew's copy off
too, so the order matters.

1. When PaceLine's release notes say that it moved the watchers to PitCrew, update PaceLine and stop
   here.
2. Otherwise write PitCrew's own settings file, which copies the values PaceLine had:

   ```
   /pitcrew:context-watch config --on
   ```

3. Then turn off PaceLine's copy:

   ```
   /paceline:context-watch config --off
   ```

4. For the cache, start a session's watch with only one of `/pitcrew:cache-watch on` and
   `/paceline:cache-watch on`. A session watched under both has two waiters.

**How to tell it worked:** `/pitcrew:context-watch status` prints `settings:` with PitCrew's file
and no `(from PaceLine)` line, `/paceline:context-watch status` shows `context-watch off`, and a
compaction writes one snapshot, in `.claude/pitcrew/`. See [PaceLine 0.6.0 or earlier runs its own
copy](limitations.md#paceline-060-or-earlier-runs-its-own-copy).
